title: Scikit-learn Pipelines and Workflow
summary: As projects grow, ad-hoc scripts become error-prone. Pipelines bundle preprocessing and modeling into a single reproducible object, ensuring the same transformations apply consistently and preventing data leakage. Cross-validation gives a more reliab
content:
# Scikit-learn Pipelines and Workflow ##### The notebook that could not be reproduced A model went to production and immediately produced nonsense. The engineer went back to the notebook that had produced 0.91 F1 in testing. Cell 4 loaded the data. Cell 11 fitted a `StandardScaler`. Cell 7 imputed missing values — but cell 7 had been re-run *after* cell 11 during a debugging session, so the scaler had been fitted on unimputed data containing NaNs. Cell 19 encoded categoricals with a fresh encoder that had never seen the production categories. And somewhere between cells 22 and 30, a `GridSearchCV` had been run on data that had already been scaled using statistics computed from the full dataset. The 0.91 was not reproducible because nobody, including the author, could reconstruct the order in which the transformations had been applied. A **Pipeline** eliminates this entire class of problem. It bundles preprocessing and modelling into one object with one `fit` and one `predict`, applied in a guaranteed order, fitted only on training data. It is the single most valuable habit in applied scikit-learn, and the reason is not tidiness — it is correctness. ##### The Pipeline object A Pipeline is a sequence of named steps. Every step except the last must be a transformer (having `fit` and `transform`); the last is usually an estimator (having `fit` and `predict`). ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression pipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)), ]) pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) # fits every step on training data, in order predictions = pipe.predict(X_test) # applies fitted transforms, then predicts ``` What happens inside `fit`: the imputer learns the training medians and transforms; the scaler learns the *resulting* means and standard deviations and transforms; the classifier trains on the output. What happens inside `predict`: the same fitted parameters are applied — no re-fitting, no test statistics involved. That is the guarantee. Test data is only ever **transformed** using parameters learned from training data, and the order can never drift because it is declared once. ##### ColumnTransformer Real datasets mix types, and numeric and categorical columns need different treatment. `ColumnTransformer` applies different pipelines to different columns in parallel: ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier numeric_features = ["age", "income", "tenure_months", "monthly_spend"] categorical_features = ["city", "plan_type", "acquisition_channel"] ordinal_features = ["satisfaction"] # low < medium < high numeric_pipeline = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ]) categorical_pipeline = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first", sparse_output=False)), ]) ordinal_pipeline = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("encode", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["low", "medium", "high"]])), ]) preprocessor = ColumnTransformer( transformers=[ ("num", numeric_pipeline, numeric_features), ("cat", categorical_pipeline, categorical_features), ("ord", ordinal_pipeline, ordinal_features), ], remainder="drop", # explicitly discard unlisted columns verbose_feature_names_out=False, ) model = Pipeline([ ("prep", preprocessor), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)), ]) ``` Two settings prevent production failures. **`handle_unknown="ignore"`** means a category appearing only at inference time encodes as all zeros rather than raising an exception — without it, one unseen city crashes your service. And **`remainder="drop"`** is explicit about unlisted columns; the alternative, `"passthrough"`, silently forwards raw columns including IDs and text, which usually breaks the model. After fitting, you can recover the expanded feature names — essential for interpreting coefficients or feature importances: ```python model.fit(X_train, y_train) feature_names = model.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out() importances = model.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_ top = pd.Series(importances, index=feature_names).nlargest(10) print(top.round(4)) ``` ##### Cross-validation A single train/test split gives one number, and that number has substantial variance — a different random seed can shift it by several points. **Cross-validation** splits the data k ways, trains k times, and reports a mean and spread. ```python from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, cross_validate, StratifiedKFold cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1) print(f"F1: {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}") print(f"Individual folds: {scores.round(3)}") ``` **Report the standard deviation.** A model scoring 0.84 ± 0.01 is meaningfully more trustworthy than one scoring 0.86 ± 0.08 — the second may simply have been lucky on one split. Choose the splitting strategy to match your data: | Strategy | Use when | |---|---| | `KFold` | Regression, balanced data | | `StratifiedKFold` | **Classification** — preserves class ratios in every fold | | `GroupKFold` | Repeated entities (multiple rows per customer) must not span folds | | `TimeSeriesSplit` | **Time-ordered data** — train on past, validate on future | | `LeaveOneOut` | Very small datasets only; expensive and high-variance | Two of these prevent specific leakage failures. **`GroupKFold`** stops the same customer appearing in both training and validation, which would let the model recognize individuals rather than learn patterns. **`TimeSeriesSplit`** never trains on data that came after the validation period: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GroupKFold tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5) # expanding window, always past → future gkf = GroupKFold(n_splits=5) # pass groups=customer_ids to cross_val_score ``` To evaluate several metrics at once and inspect training scores for overfitting: ```python results = cross_validate( model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"], return_train_score=True, n_jobs=-1, ) for metric in ["f1", "roc_auc"]: tr = results[f"train_{metric}"].mean() te = results[f"test_{metric}"].mean() print(f"{metric:<9} train {tr:.3f} val {te:.3f} gap {tr - te:+.3f}") ``` That gap column is your overfitting diagnostic, computed across five folds rather than one lucky split. ##### Grid search and random search Hyperparameters are the settings you choose rather than learn — tree depth, regularization strength, number of neighbours. Tuning them systematically beats guessing. **GridSearchCV** tries every combination: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV param_grid = { "prep__num__impute__strategy": ["median", "mean"], "clf__n_estimators": [100, 300, 500], "clf__max_depth": [5, 10, 20, None], "clf__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20], } grid = GridSearchCV( model, param_grid, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1, verbose=1, refit=True, return_train_score=True, ) grid.fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"Best F1: {grid.best_score_:.3f}") print(f"Best params: {grid.best_params_}") best_model = grid.best_estimator_ # already refitted on all training data ``` Note the **double-underscore syntax**: `clf__max_depth` means "the `max_depth` parameter of the step named `clf`." Nested pipelines chain further — `prep__num__impute__strategy` reaches into the preprocessor, then the numeric pipeline, then the imputer. This is how you tune preprocessing choices alongside model hyperparameters, which is genuinely useful and impossible without a Pipeline. That grid has 2 × 3 × 4 × 3 = 72 combinations × 5 folds = **360 model fits**. Grid search grows multiplicatively, and it quickly becomes impractical. **RandomizedSearchCV** samples a fixed number of combinations from distributions instead: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV from scipy.stats import randint, uniform param_dist = { "clf__n_estimators": randint(100, 800), "clf__max_depth": randint(3, 30), "clf__min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 40), "clf__max_features": uniform(0.1, 0.9), } search = RandomizedSearchCV( model, param_dist, n_iter=60, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1, random_state=42, refit=True, ) search.fit(X_train, y_train) ``` Random search usually finds comparable results in far fewer fits. The reason is that most hyperparameters barely matter while a few matter a great deal — grid search wastes evaluations on fine-grained variation in unimportant dimensions, while random search explores the important ones more broadly. **Use random search for a wide initial sweep, then a small grid around the promising region.** For larger budgets, `HalvingRandomSearchCV` uses successive halving — evaluating many candidates on small data subsets and promoting only the survivors — which is substantially faster. ##### Saving and loading models ```python import joblib from pathlib import Path Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True) joblib.dump(best_model, "models/churn_v1.joblib", compress=3) # Save metadata alongside it — a model without provenance is a liability metadata = { "version": "1.0.0", "trained_at": pd.Timestamp.now().isoformat(), "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, "cv_f1_mean": float(grid.best_score_), "test_f1": float(f1_score(y_test, best_model.predict(X_test))), "params": grid.best_params_, "feature_columns": list(X_train.columns), "n_training_samples": len(X_train), } Path("models/churn_v1.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2, default=str)) # Later, at inference time loaded = joblib.load("models/churn_v1.joblib") predictions = loaded.predict(new_data) # ALL preprocessing applied automatically ``` The decisive advantage: **you save the whole pipeline, not just the model.** At inference time there is nothing to remember — no separate scaler to load, no encoder to reconstruct, no order to get right. One object, one `predict` call, identical transformations. Prefer `joblib` over `pickle` for scikit-learn — it handles large NumPy arrays more efficiently. And record the scikit-learn version, because unpickling a model saved under a different version can fail or, worse, behave subtly differently. ##### Why pipelines prevent leakage This is the assignment's question, and the mechanism deserves precision. Consider scaling before cross-validation, done manually: ```python # WRONG — leakage X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) # mean/std from ALL data scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_scaled, y, cv=5) ``` The scaler computed its mean and standard deviation using **every row, including the rows that will become validation folds**. Each validation fold is therefore scaled using statistics that partly describe itself. The model is evaluated on data that influenced its own preprocessing, and the resulting score is optimistically biased. ```python # CORRECT — no leakage pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression())]) scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5) ``` Now, inside each of the five folds, `cross_val_score` calls `pipe.fit()` on that fold's training portion only. The scaler learns from four-fifths of the data and transforms the held-out fifth. Five folds, five independently fitted scalers, no contamination. The bias is often small for scaling and large for imputation and target encoding — but it is always in the same direction, and it is invisible. You get a score you cannot reproduce in production, exactly like the opening story. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Raw data] --> B[train_test_split
test set sealed] B --> C[Training data] C --> D[Pipeline: preprocessor + model] D --> E[GridSearch / RandomizedSearch
with cross-validation] E --> F["Inside EACH fold:
fit transforms on 4/5
transform the held-out 1/5"] F --> G[Best params + refit on
all training data] G --> H[Evaluate ONCE on test set] H --> I[joblib.dump pipeline
+ metadata JSON] I --> J[Production: load, predict
preprocessing included] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Preprocessing outside the pipeline**, then cross-validating — the classic leakage. - **`fit_transform` on test data** instead of `transform`. - **`KFold` for classification** instead of `StratifiedKFold`. - **Random splits on time-series or grouped data.** - **Reporting only the mean CV score** without the spread. - **Tuning against the test set** by repeatedly evaluating and adjusting. - **Grid search over huge spaces** where random search would be far cheaper. - **Saving only the estimator**, losing the preprocessing. - **No metadata with the saved model** — no version, no training date, no expected columns. - **Forgetting `handle_unknown="ignore"`**, so an unseen category crashes production. - **Overfitting to the CV score** by trying hundreds of configurations; the winning score becomes optimistic. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a **Pipeline combining preprocessing and a classifier**, then use **GridSearchCV with cross-validation** to tune it. Include at least one preprocessing hyperparameter in the grid (imputation strategy is a good choice) — it demonstrates the double-underscore syntax and shows why bundling preprocessing into the pipeline gives you more to tune, not less. The mini project is an **end-to-end reproducible pipeline** that loads data, preprocesses, tunes, evaluates via cross-validation, and **saves the best model to disk**. Then prove the reproducibility claim: restart the kernel, load the saved pipeline, and predict on raw unprocessed data. If it works without you re-creating a single transformer, the pipeline is doing its job. For the assignment, **explain why wrapping preprocessing inside a pipeline prevents leakage during cross-validation**. Do not just assert it — demonstrate it. Run the same model both ways on the same data and report both scores. The manual version will score higher, and that gap *is* the leakage, quantified. Showing a measured difference is far more convincing than describing a mechanism. ##### Key takeaways - A Pipeline bundles preprocessing and modelling into one object with a guaranteed order, fitted on training data only — correctness, not tidiness, is the reason. - `ColumnTransformer` applies different treatment to numeric, categorical and ordinal columns; always set `handle_unknown="ignore"` and be explicit about `remainder`. - Cross-validate with the strategy your data demands — stratified for classification, grouped for repeated entities, time-series for ordered data — and report the spread alongside the mean. - Use random search for wide sweeps and grid search to refine; the `step__param` syntax lets you tune preprocessing choices too. - Save the entire fitted pipeline with `joblib` plus a metadata file, so inference applies identical transformations with no steps to remember.
